subject: forensic-medicine
title: Identification: Dactylography, Fingerprint Patterns and Poroscopy

steps.title: The scientific foundation of dactylography
steps.tx: Pioneered by Sir William Herschel, Sir Francis Galton, and Sir Edward Henry, the **dactylography forensic identification system** represents the study of epidermal friction ridges on fingertips. Dactylography rests on two immutable biological principles: absolute uniqueness, meaning no two individuals or fingers have identical patterns, and permanence, as ridge patterns develop by the fourth intrauterine month and remain unchanged throughout life until postmortem decomposition.
steps.say: Dactylography is the study of finger ridge patterns, which are completely unique and permanent from the fourth fetal month until decomposition.

steps.title: The four primary Galton fingerprint patterns
steps.tx: In dermatoglyphic classification, every human fingerprint conforms to one of the **four Galton pattern types**, categorized by ridge architecture and focal cores. Loops represent the most prevalent pattern, accounting for sixty to sixty-five percent of prints. Whorls constitute twenty-five to thirty percent, arches represent five to seven percent, and composite or accidental patterns comprise the remaining two to three percent of friction ridge configurations.
steps.say: Fingerprints divide into four patterns: loops form sixty-five percent, whorls thirty percent, arches five to seven percent, and composites two to three percent.

steps.title: Loop patterns: Ulnar loops versus radial loops
steps.tx: Characterized by flowing ridges that enter, recurve, and exit on the same side, the **loop fingerprint architectural pattern** possesses exactly one triradius delta and one central core. Forensic examiners classify loops based on ridge exit direction relative to forearm bones: an ulnar loop flows toward the little finger (ulna), while a radial loop opens toward the thumb (radius), with ulnar loops predominating overwhelmingly.
steps.say: Loops have one delta and one core. An ulnar loop opens toward the little finger, while a radial loop opens toward the thumb.

steps.title: Whorl patterns and delta formations
steps.tx: Demonstrating complex circular dynamics, the **whorl fingerprint ridge structure** possesses at least two triradius deltas and a central core surrounded by complete circuit ridges. The concentric ridges may form concentric rings, expanding spirals, or target-like circular patterns. Subtypes include central pocket loops, double loop whorls comprising two interlocking loops, and accidental whorls combining multiple divergent patterns that resist standard categorization.
steps.say: Whorls feature circular or spiral ridges with at least two deltas and a core, including plain whorls, double loops, and accidental configurations.

steps.title: Arch patterns: Plain arches and tented arches
steps.tx: Representing the simplest yet rarest configuration, the **arch fingerprint ridge structure** is characterized by complete absence of deltas and cores. Ridges enter from one side of the fingertip, rise in the center forming a smooth wave, and exit smoothly on the opposite side. Plain arches display gentle wave-like elevations, whereas tented arches display a sharp vertical central spike resembling an erect tent pole.
steps.say: Arches have no deltas or cores. Ridges enter one side, rise in the middle, and exit the other side, forming plain waves or sharp tented spikes.

steps.title: Minutiae characteristics and legal matching standards
steps.tx: Individual fingerprint identification does not rely on gross patterns alone, but on microscopic **individual ridge minutiae characteristics**, also known as Galton details. Minutiae comprise ridge endings, bifurcations (Y-shaped splitting), islands (independent short ridges), enclosures (lakes), dots, bridges, and spurs. Under Indian judicial practice, demonstrating sixteen matching minutiae with identical relative spatial positions establishes incontrovertible, conclusive legal identification in court.
steps.say: Conclusive identification relies on minutiae like ridge endings, bifurcations, and islands. In Indian courts, sixteen matching minutiae provide proof of identity.

steps.title: Poroscopy: Locard's microscopic pore identification
steps.tx: Pioneered by Edmond Locard, the science of **poroscopy sweat pore analysis** examines the microscopic pores of sweat gland ducts opening along friction ridges. There are nine to eighteen pores per linear millimeter of ridge. Pores vary in size, spatial interval, and geometric shape (round, oval, triangular). Because pore configurations never change, finding twenty to forty identical pores identifies an individual even from partial fragments.
steps.say: Poroscopy examines microscopic sweat gland pores along ridges. Finding twenty to forty matching pores confirms identity even from small partial prints.

steps.title: Edgeoscopy and modern automated biometric systems
steps.tx: Complementing poroscopy, the discipline of **edgeoscopy ridge contour analysis** examines microscopic morphological irregularities, indentations, and notches along the lateral borders of friction ridges. In modern crime laboratories, these features integrate into the Automated Fingerprint Identification System (AFIS), which digitizes latent crime scene prints, maps minutiae coordinate vectors, and scans millions of national criminal records within seconds.
steps.say: Edgeoscopy examines irregular ridge borders, working alongside computerized AFIS databases that match latent crime scene prints against national databases.

steps.title: Latent fingerprint development methods
steps.tx: At crime scenes, invisible **latent fingerprint chemical development** techniques visualize deposited sebaceous oils and eccrine sweat residues. Non-porous surfaces like glass or metal are developed using black powder dusting, magnetic powders, or cyanoacrylate superglue fuming. Porous documents, paper notes, or cardboard are treated with ninhydrin spraying (reacting with amino acids to form Ruhemann purple) or silver nitrate reacting with sodium chloride.
steps.say: Latent prints are developed with black powder or superglue fuming on smooth surfaces, and ninhydrin spray on paper, revealing invisible sweat deposits.
